name: George Müller
title: George Müller: prayer and the everyday care of orphaned children
description: George Müller and the Bristol orphan homes from 1836 onward: history and autobiographical testimony, with identified sources.

sections.heading: The need had names and faces
paragraphs: In 1836, George Müller’s work with orphaned children in Bristol began. The overview at GeorgeMuller.org dates the opening of the first home to April of that year. The project responded to concrete needs for care and was bound up with Müller’s conviction that he should depend on God to sustain it.

The growth of the homes required houses, staff and organization. Although his story is often summed up in episodes of prayer, the ministry involved daily tasks: taking in the children, feeding them, caring for them and preparing them for the future. A lasting institution carries responsibilities that go well beyond the moment a donation is received.

sections.heading: How to read his accounts of provision
paragraphs: In his autobiography, Müller kept records of needs, income and answers that he understood as God’s provision. It is a valuable primary source for knowing how he understood his work. Its autobiographical character should remain in view: we are reading the testimony of a participant, not an independent confirmation of each spiritual explanation.

The accounts and material details in that record show that religious trust went hand in hand with administration. Here we avoid repeating, unchecked, the popular breakfast scene and the food that supposedly arrived at the last moment. His legacy can be told from his documented work without relying on an anecdote whose exact version has not been verified.

reflection: James 2:14–17 links faith with help that meets material needs. Müller’s story lets us reflect on that connection: praying for a child includes recognizing that he or she needs food, safety and care. Trust in God can go together with responsible and lasting care.

For a church that wants to serve, the account raises practical questions: who will take on the care, how resources will be managed and how accounts will be given. Prayer and planning can walk together. A story of provision should help us care for people better, without promising that every institution will always receive what it needs through the same method.
review_note: The viral breakfast anecdote is left out; interpretations of provision are attributed to the autobiographical testimony. No universal funding method is promised.
source_labels: Ed Reese. “The Life & Ministry of George Muller” (June 29, 2016), published at GeorgeMuller.org.
